s: Leonidas of Rhodes wins Olympian games (twelve times in four Olympiads)
q: in four Olympiads he was in his prime, and 12 times conqueror through his swiftness of foot.

s: Astylus of Croton wins at Olympian games (three successive Olympiads)
q: he was victorious at three Olympiads in succession in the stade and in the double course.

s: Mnaseas has statue by Pythagoras (sculptor from Rhegium)
q: by Pythagoras of Rhegium.

s: mare of Phidolas has statue Olympian games
q: And the people of Elis proclaimed Phidolas victor, and allowed him to set up a statue of this mare.

s: Nicasylus wins at Isthmian games (after winning at Olympia)
q: He was proclaimed victor also at the Nemean and Isthmian games.

s: Artemidorus of Tralles wins the victory among men (at Olympia in the 212th Olympiad)
q: And Artemidorus won at Olympia the victory among men in the 212th Olympiad.

s: Artemidorus of Tralles wins the victory among men (at Olympia in the 212th Olympiad)
q: And Artemidorus won at Olympia the victory among men in the 212th Olympiad.

s: Milo is a wrestling victor (from Croton)
q: This Milo had six prizes for wrestling at Olympia, one of them among boys, and at Pythia six among men and one among boys.

s: Milo wins in wrestling (six prizes at Olympia, including one among boys)
q: This Milo had six prizes for wrestling at Olympia, one of them among boys

s: Milo wins at Pythian games (six victories among men and one among boys)
q: and at Pythia six among men and one among boys.

s: Milo loses to Timasitheus (in his seventh Olympic wrestling attempt)
q: But he could not beat in wrestling Timasitheus, a citizen and quite young

s: Milo has statue by Dameas (both were natives of Croton)
q: And the statue of Milo the son of Diotimus is by Dameas, both natives of Croton.

s: Milo is son of Diotimus
q: the statue of Milo the son of Diotimus

s: Milo’s statue is carried by Milo (according to tradition)
q: And Milo is said to have carried his own statue to Altis.

s: Pyrrhus is a king (of Thesprotia in Epirus)
q: And Pyrrhus the son of Æacides having been king in Thesprotia in Epirus

s: Pyrrhus has statue by Thrasybulus of Elis (statue erected in Altis)
q: Thrasybulus of Elis erected his statue in Altis.

s: Pythes has statue by Lysippus (two statues made at the request of his soldiers)
q: the two statues of Pythes, the son of Andromachus, an Abderite, were made by Lysippus, but his soldiers had them made.

s: Tisamenus is a prophet (prophet for the Greeks against Mardonius and the Medes at Plataea)
q: that Tisamenus who was afterwards a prophet for the Greeks against Mardonius and the Medes at Platæa.

s: Clitomachus of Thebes has statue statue (erected by Hermocrates his father)
q: And the statue of Clitomachus the Theban was erected by Hermocrates his father.

s: Clitomachus of Thebes is son of Hermocrates
q: the statue of Clitomachus the Theban was erected by Hermocrates his father.

s: Clitomachus of Thebes wins in wrestling (at the Isthmian games)
q: In the Isthmian games he beat all comers in wrestling

s: Clitomachus of Thebes wins in boxing (at the Isthmian games, on one day with wrestling and pancratium victories)
q: and on one day won prizes from all competitors in boxing and in the pancratium.

s: Clitomachus of Thebes wins in pancratium (three Pythian victories; one Olympic victory in the 141st Olympiad)
q: And all his 3 victories in the Pythian games were in the pancratium. And at Olympia he was proclaimed second to Theagenes of Thasos in the pancratium and in boxing. And in the 141st Olympiad he won the prize in the pancratium.

s: Clitomachus of Thebes loses to Caprus of Elis (in the pancratium after Caprus won wrestling)
q: when the pancratium was called on he was beaten by Caprus

s: Caprus of Elis is a wrestling and pancratium victor (won both prizes on the same day)
q: Caprus of Elis, the son of Pythagoras, who won on the same day for the first time on record prizes for wrestling and the pancratium.

s: Caprus of Elis is son of Pythagoras
q: Caprus of Elis, the son of Pythagoras

s: Demetrius is a military commander (led an army against Seleucus and was captured in battle)
q: the statues of Demetrius, who led an army against Seleucus and was taken prisoner in the battle

s: Antigonus son of Demetrius is son of Demetrius
q: and of Antigonus the son of Demetrius

s: Altis contains statues and votive offerings (in the area approached from Leonidas’ monument toward the great altar)
q: What I have just mentioned are the most notable things as you approach Altis, but, if you go on the right from the monument of Leonidas to the great altar, you will behold the following memorable objects.

s: Anaximenes of Lampsacus is a sophist (a very good imitator of sophists’ arguments)
q: He was naturally a sophist and a very good imitator of the arguments of the sophists.

s: Anaximenes of Lampsacus practises extempore oratory (said to be the first practitioner)
q: Nor did any one earlier than Anaximenes practise extempore oratory.

s: people of Lampsacus are pardoned by Alexander (after Anaximenes’ stratagem)
q: and Alexander having no contrivance to meet his cunning, and being compelled by his oath, very unwillingly pardoned the people of Lampsacus.

s: Mount Cronos is behind treasuries of Olympia (extending along their length)
q: Cronos’ mountain is, as I have already said, behind the base, and extends the length of these treasuries.

s: treasuries of Olympia is located on a base of tufa stone (to the North of the temple of Hera)
q: And there is in Altis a base of tufa stone to the North of the temple of Hera, at its back is the mountain of Cronos. On this base are treasuries such as some of the Greeks have made for Apollo at Delphi.

s: treasury of the Sicyonians is a treasury (at Olympia)
q: There is a treasury at Olympia called the treasury of the Sicyonians, the votive offering of Myron the King of the Sicyonians.

s: treasury of the Sicyonians is built by Myron (after his chariot victory)
q: It was constructed by Myron after his chariot victory in the 33rd Olympiad.

s: treasury of the Sicyonians has chamber two chambers (one Doric and one Ionic)
q: In this treasury he constructed two chambers, one of Doric the other of Ionic architecture.

s: treasury of the Sicyonians contains shield of the Myanes (with helmet and greaves to match)
q: And there is a brazen shield curiously painted inside, and helmet and greaves to match. And there is an inscription on this armour that they are an offering to Zeus from the Myanes.

s: Olympia contains treasuries of Olympia (on a tufa-stone base north of the temple of Hera)
q: And there is in Altis a base of tufa stone to the North of the temple of Hera, at its back is the mountain of Cronos. On this base are treasuries such as some of the Greeks have made for Apollo at Delphi.

s: treasury of the Sicyonians contains sword of Pelops (with a golden hilt)
q: There are also here several other curious articles, as the sword of Pelops with golden hilt, and the horn of Amalthea in ivory, the votive offering of Miltiades the son of Cimon, who was the first of his family that reigned in the Thracian Chersonese

s: treasury of the Sicyonians contains horn of Amalthea (made of ivory)
q: There are also here several other curious articles, as the sword of Pelops with golden hilt, and the horn of Amalthea in ivory, the votive offering of Miltiades the son of Cimon, who was the first of his family that reigned in the Thracian Chersonese

s: treasury of the Sicyonians contains Apollo (a boxwood statue with gilt head)
q: There is also a statue of Apollo made of boxwood with the head gilt: the inscription states that it was a votive offering of the Locrians at the promontory of Zephyrium, and by Patrocles of Croton, the son of Catillus.

s: Ilithyia has temple at Olympia (at the north end of Mount Cronos)
q: And at the North end of Mount Cronos there is between the treasuries and the mountain a temple of Ilithyia, and in it is honoured Sosipolis the tutelary deity of the people of Elis.

s: Ilithyia is surnamed Olympian
q: Ilithyia they surname the Olympian, and select annually a priestess for her: the old priestess of Sosipolis also performs holy rites according to the custom of the people of Elis

s: Sosipolis is a tutelary deity (of the people of Elis)
q: And at the North end of Mount Cronos there is between the treasuries and the mountain a temple of Ilithyia, and in it is honoured Sosipolis the tutelary deity of the people of Elis.

s: Sosipolis is honored in temple of Ilithyia (inside the sanctuary, inaccessible except to his priestess)
q: In the vestibule of the temple is the altar of Ilithyia, as also the approach to the temple for people generally: inside Sosipolis is honoured, and no one but the priestess of the god must enter his sanctuary, with a white veil drawn over her head and face.

s: Sosipolis receives hymns and incense (from maidens and women; no wine libations)
q: And the maidens that reside in the temple of Ilithyia and the women sing hymns to Sosipolis, and burn incense to him, but are not accustomed to pour libations of wine to his honour.

s: Elis worships Sosipolis (as its tutelary deity)
q: And at the North end of Mount Cronos there is between the treasuries and the mountain a temple of Ilithyia, and in it is honoured Sosipolis the tutelary deity of the people of Elis.

s: Hippodamium is a walled precinct (inside Altis, occupying about an acre)
q: And inside Altis, at the processional entrance, is what is called the Hippodamium, surrounded by a wall, occupying about an acre.

s: Gorgias of Leontini is a rhetorician (said to have been the first practitioner of rhetoric)
q: This Gorgias was the son of Carmantides, and is said to have been the first to have practised Rhetoric, which had been altogether neglected and nearly come into desuetude among men.

s: Hippodamium receives women (annually for rites honoring Hippodamia)
q: This is the entrance every year for the women, who sacrifice to Hippodamia and perform other rites in her honour.

s: Hippodamia receives rites at Hippodamium (including sacrifices by women)
q: This is the entrance every year for the women, who sacrifice to Hippodamia and perform other rites in her honour.

s: Olympian games are watched by Demeter (through her priestess seated on a white-stone altar)
q: And opposite the Umpires is an altar of white stone, seated on which the priestess of Demeter Chamyne watches the Olympian games, an honour which different priestesses at different times have received from the people of Elis, for they do not prevent maidens from seeing the games.

s: horse-race starting-place is shaped like prow of a ship (with its beak turned toward the course)
q: And near the place where the Umpires sit is the ground appointed for the horse-races and the starting-place, which is in shape like the prow of a ship with its beak turned to the course.

s: horse-race starting-place has length more than 400 feet on each side
q: Each side of the starting-place is more than 400 feet in length, and there are some buildings there, which those who enter for the horse-races get by lots.

s: horse-race starting-place contains brazen dolphin (mounted on a bar at the extremity of the beak)
q: And there is a brazen dolphin upon a bar at the extremity of the beak.

s: Agnaptus Portico is adjacent to horse-race starting-place (the starting-place is broad where it joins the portico)
q: And the prow is broad where it joins the Portico called Agnaptus.

s: horse-races use horse-race starting-place (with staggered releases to ensure a fair start)
q: First the ropes on each side of the Portico called Agnaptus are slackened, and the horses in position there start first, and run on till they come to the horses in the second position, and then the ropes there are slackened, and so on along the whole course where the horses are in position, till they can all start fair at the beak.

s: Gorgias of Leontini has statue at Olympia (placed there by Eumolpus)
q: And there are some statues interspersed among some not very remarkable votive offerings, as Alexinicus of Elis (by the Sicyonian Cantharus), who won a wrestling prize among the boys, and Gorgias of Leontini, whose statue was placed at Olympia by Eumolpus, great-grandson of Deicrates who had married Gorgias’ sister.

s: horse-races are associated with Taraxippus (a source of terror to horses at the outlet of the course)
q: But the other side of the Hippodrome is more extended, being also of raised earth, and at its outlet is Taraxippus the terror of horses, which is in the shape of a circular altar, and as the horses run past it they are immediately seized with strong fear without any apparent cause

s: Taraxippus is a circular altar (at the outlet of the Hippodrome)
q: But the other side of the Hippodrome is more extended, being also of raised earth, and at its outlet is Taraxippus the terror of horses, which is in the shape of a circular altar

s: Taraxippus terrifies horses (causing panic, wrecked chariots and injuries to charioteers)
q: and as the horses run past it they are immediately seized with strong fear without any apparent cause, and this fear generates terror, insomuch that chariots are often smashed up, and the charioteers badly injured.

s: Taraxippus is identified with Poseidon (the most plausible interpretation)
q: The most plausible account however of Taraxippus seems to me that which makes it a surname of Poseidon Hippius.

s: battle between the Eleans and Arcadians results in victory for Elis (after Sosipolis appeared as a dragon)
q: And the Arcadians commenced the attack, and the child was changed into a dragon, and the Arcadians were troubled at the sight and began to flee, and the people of Elis pursued them hotly, and won a notable victory and called the god Sosipolis.

s: battle between the Eleans and Arcadians has monument for Arcadians (the slain were commemorated west of the Cladeus)
q: And the Arcadians who were slain in the battle have a monument on the hill towards the west after you have crossed the Cladeus.

s: Arcadians invade Elis (with an army)
q: And it is said that, when the Arcadians invaded Elis with an army, and the people of Elis were drawn up in battle array against them, a woman came to the generals of Elis, with a baby boy at her breast

s: Arcadians are defeated by Elis (in the battle associated with Sosipolis)
q: And the Arcadians commenced the attack, and the child was changed into a dragon, and the Arcadians were troubled at the sight and began to flee, and the people of Elis pursued them hotly, and won a notable victory and called the god Sosipolis.

s: Gorgias of Leontini is son of Carmantides
q: This Gorgias was the son of Carmantides, and is said to have been the first to have practised Rhetoric, which had been altogether neglected and nearly come into desuetude among men.

s: Gorgias of Leontini has lifespan 105 years (according to report)
q: And they say Gorgias lived 105 years.

s: Anaximenes of Lampsacus is a historian (wrote histories of Greece, Philip and Alexander)
q: Here too I found the statue of Anaximenes, who wrote a History of all Antiquities in Greece, and of the exploits of Philip the son of Amyntas, and afterwards of Alexander.

s: Anaximenes of Lampsacus has statue at Olympia (honored by the people of Lampsacus)
q: This honour in Olympia he owed to the people of Lampsacus: for the following is recorded about him.

s: Demeter is a Demeter (worshipped under this name)
q: on the top of which is a temple built to Demeter under the name of Chamyne.

s: gymnasium at Olympia is used for pentathlum (athletes practise there)
q: in the gymnasium at Olympia they practise for the pentathlum and the races.

s: Arcadia has boundary at Olympia (boundaries now belong to Elis but formerly to Pisa)
q: And here are the boundaries towards Arcadia, which now belong to the people of Elis, but formerly belonged to the people of Pisa.

s: Saurus is killed by Hercules (after molesting travellers and local people)
q: Saurus they say used to molest wayfarers and the people of the country, till he was killed by Hercules.

s: Diagon divides Pisa (from Arcadia)
q: Its name is Diagon, and it divides the district of Pisa from Arcadia.

s: Lucyanias flows into Alpheus (rises in Mount Pholoe)
q: the river Lucyanias, which rises in Mount Pholoe, and flows into the Alpheus.

s: Athene has temple at Phrixa (only an altar survives in the author's time)
q: on it are ruins of the town of Phrixa, and a temple of Athene Cydonia, not in my time in complete preservation, there is only an altar.

s: Pelops sacrifices to Athene (before racing Oenomaus, according to Elis tradition)
q: The people of Elis say also that Pelops sacrificed to Athene Cydonia before his race with Œnomaus.

s: suitors of Hippodamia has tomb all these
q: Here then is the tomb of all these, and they say Pelops offered them funeral rites every year when he was king of Pisa.

s: Pelops buries suitors of Hippodamia (in a common sepulchre, in honour and affection)
q: it was Pelops subsequently who gave them a common sepulchre, in honour to them and out of affection to Hippodamia

s: Great Eoeae states were killed by suitors of Hippodamia
q: Indeed according to the poem called the Great Eœæ the following were killed by Œnomaus

s: Artemis is worshipped at temple of Artemis Cordace (the attendants of Pelops sacrifice and dance there)
q: there are traces of a temple of Artemis surnamed Cordace, because the attendants of Pelops used to offer their sacrifices to the goddess there, and dance the national dance of Sipylus called the

s: Pluto is taken in by the earth
q: the earth opened there and took in the chariot of Pluto, and closed again.

s: coffer containing Pelops's remains contains Pelops (contains his remains)
q: in it is a brazen coffer, in which are deposited the remains of Pelops.

s: Pisa is founded by Pisus (Pisus is son of Perieres and grandson of Aeolus)
q: The founder of the town was they say Pisus, the son of Perieres and grandson of Æolus.

s: Pisa is destroyed by Elis (after conflict over control of the Olympic games)
q: And the people of Elis eventually razed Pisa to the ground and all the towns that had assisted her in the war.

s: Phido patronizes Olympian games (at the eighth Olympiad)
q: they invited Phido the Argive, the most haughty of all the Greek tyrants, and made him the patron of the games.

s: Olympian games are contested by Pisa (Pisa sought to start them instead of Elis)
q: their desire to start the Olympian games instead of the people of Elis

s: Macistus joins Pisa (in revolt from Elis)
q: the people of Macistus and Scillus in Triphylia joined them in their revolt from the people of Elis

s: Scillus is situated in Triphylia
q: the people of Macistus and Scillus in Triphylia joined them in their revolt from the people of Elis

s: Dyspontii has friendly relations with Pisa
q: of the other neighbouring people the Dyspontii, whose relations had always been very friendly with the people of Pisa

s: Pylos in Elis is destroyed by Hercules (later repopulated by Elis and again left uninhabited)
q: This Pylos was built, as I have already mentioned, by the Megarian Pylon the son of Cleson. And being destroyed by Hercules, and once again peopled by the people of Elis, it was destined once more to lack inhabitants.

s: Alphean Artemis is called after Alpheus (because of his passion for her, according to one legend)
q: So the people of Letrini called the goddess Alphean from Alpheus’ passion for her.

s: Alpheus is in love with Alphean Artemis (according to the Letrini legend)
q: Alpheus they say was deeply in love with her

s: gymnasium of Elis is a gymnasium (used for training athletes before Olympia)
q: the notable things in Elis are an old gymnasium, in which before they go to Olympia the athletes go through all the customary training.

s: Proserpine has statue with Demeter (new statues erected in place of older ones)
q: in lieu of the old ones new statues of Proserpine and Demeter were erected in Pentelican marble by the Athenian Herodes.

s: Colonnade is named after Hercules (because he exercised there)
q: because Hercules the son of Amphitryon used to exercise there

s: Eros has altar in gymnasium of Elis
q: there are in the gymnasium altars to some of the gods, as Idæan Hercules under the title of Champion, and Eros, and the god whom the Athenians and people of Elis alike call Anteros

s: Anteros has altar in gymnasium of Elis
q: there are in the gymnasium altars to some of the gods, as Idæan Hercules under the title of Champion, and Eros, and the god whom the Athenians and people of Elis alike call Anteros

s: Artemis the Lover of Youths is near gymnasium of Elis
q: You go from the gymnasium to the baths by the street called Silence near the temple of Artemis the Lover of Youths.

s: market-place of Elis is called Hippodrome of Elis (in the author's time)
q: the name of the market-place in our day is Hippodrome, and there the people of the place exercise their horses.

s: market-place of Elis has Corcyraean Portico (a Doric portico near the portico where umpires spend the day)
q: near the portico where the Umpires spend the day is another portico, called the Corcyræan

s: Apollo has temple in market-place of Elis (the temple and statue are described as noble)
q: the people of Elis have in the open air near the market-place a most noble temple and statue of Apollo the Healer.

s: Graces have temple in market-place of Elis (their wooden statues have gilt dresses and marble extremities)
q: There is also a temple to the Graces, and their wooden statues, their dresses gilt, and their heads hands and feet of white marble

s: Graces are associated with Aphrodite (through their intimate connection with her)
q: The rose and myrtle are sacred to Aphrodite, and have a place in the legend of Adonis, and the Graces have most intimate connection with Aphrodite

s: Silenus has temple in market-place of Elis (the temple is dedicated to Silenus alone)
q: There is also there a temple of Silenus, dedicated to Silenus alone, and not in common to him and Dionysus

s: Fortune has temple in Elis (a huge wooden statue stands in its portico)
q: The people of Elis have also a temple to Fortune, and in the portico of this temple is a huge statue of wood

s: Sosipolis is honoured near Fortune (in a small shrine to Fortune's left)
q: Here too Sosipolis is honoured on the left of Fortune, in a rather small shrine

s: Sosipolis holds horn of Amalthea (in the representation seen in a dream)
q: represented, according to the appearance of him seen in a dream, as a boy with a particoloured cloak on covered with stars, and in one of his hands the horn of Amalthea.

s: flagons (Thyia chapel) contain wine (on the day after deposition)
q: And the next day they come to the chapel to observe the miracle, and on entering find the flagons full of wine.

s: wine flows spontaneously from temple of Dionysus (annually at the feast of Dionysus on Andros)
q: The people of Andros also say that annually at the feast of Dionysus wine flows spontaneously from the temple.

s: people of Elis have citadel at Elis (within Elis)
q: And in the citadel at Elis is a temple of Athene,

s: temple of Athene has statue of Athene (ivory and gold)
q: her statue is of ivory and gold, and said to be by Phidias,

s: statue of Athene is by Phidias (said to be)
q: her statue is of ivory and gold, and said to be by Phidias,

s: cock is sacred to Athene (perhaps as Athene the Worker)
q: or perhaps because it is sacred to Athene the Worker.

s: Cyllene is a harbour (fine; faces Sicily)
q: Cyllene, which faces Sicily, and is a fine harbour for ships.

s: Cyllene faces Sicily
q: Cyllene, which faces Sicily, and is a fine harbour for ships.

s: dockyard of Elis belongs to people of Elis
q: The dockyard belongs to the people of Elis

s: Cyllene has name from Arcadian
q: but got its name from an Arcadian.

s: Homer knows Cyllene (as shown subsequently in the Iliad)
q: Homer has not mentioned Cyllene in his Catalogue of the people of Elis, but subsequently in the Iliad shews that he knew that there was such a town as Cyllene.

s: Iliad mentions Cyllene (subsequently to the Catalogue of the people of Elis)
q: but subsequently in the Iliad shews that he knew that there was such a town as Cyllene.

s: Cyllene has temple of Æsculapius
q: The gods who have temples in Cyllene are Æsculapius and Aphrodite.

s: Cyllene has temple of Aphrodite
q: The gods who have temples in Cyllene are Æsculapius and Aphrodite.

s: Ithyphallic statue of Hermes is in Cyllene
q: Hermes also has an Ithyphallic statue, which the natives pay extravagant honour to.

s: Elis is fertile in fruits (of all kinds)
q: The country of Elis is fertile in fruits of all kinds but especially in flax.

s: Elis is fertile in flax (especially)
q: The country of Elis is fertile in fruits of all kinds but especially in flax.

s: Seres produce threads (for garments)
q: But the threads which the Seres make their garments of are not from any plant, but are produced in the following manner.

s: Ser is a insect (called Ser by the Greeks)
q: There is an insect on the earth which the Greeks called Ser, but the Seres give it another name.

s: Ser resembles spiders (in other respects; about twice the size of the largest beetle)
q: Its size is about double that of the largest beetle, and in other respects it is like the spiders that weave their webs under trees, and has also 8 feet like spiders.

s: Seres breed Ser
q: These insects the Seres breed, and put summer and winter into little domiciles specially constructed for them.

s: Ser lives in domiciles for the Ser (through summer and winter)
q: These insects the Seres breed, and put summer and winter into little domiciles specially constructed for them.

s: Dionysus has statue by Praxiteles
q: the statue of the god is by Praxiteles.

s: Ser produces threads (a slender thread rolling round its feet)
q: And what these insects produce is a slender thread, which rolls round their feet.

s: Ser is fed grain (for four years)
q: For 4 years they feed them on grain,

s: Ser is fed green reed (in the fifth year)
q: and in the fifth year (for they know they will not live longer) they give them green reed to eat.

s: Ser dies after five years (according to the Seres' knowledge)
q: and in the fifth year (for they know they will not live longer) they give them green reed to eat.

s: Seria is an island in Red Sea (according to a well-known report)
q: It is well-known that the island Seria is in the Red Sea.

s: Seria is formed by river Ser (according to another report, not by the Red Sea)
q: But I have heard that it is not the Red Sea, but a river called the Ser that makes this island, just as in Egypt the Delta is formed by the Nile and not by sea.

s: Seres are of race Ethiopian (according to one tradition)
q: The Seres are of Ethiopian race,

s: Seres are a cross breed of Scythians and Indians (according to another tradition)
q: Some however say that they are not Ethiopians but a cross-breed of Scythians and Indians.

s: people of Elis honour Dionysus (most of all the gods)
q: And of all the gods the people of Elis honour Dionysus most,

s: Achaia is reached from Elis (by traveling about 127 stades to the river Larisus)
q: As you go from Elis to Achaia it is about 127 stades to the river Larisus,

s: Dionysus frequents Thyia (according to the people of Elis)
q: and say that he frequents their festival in his honour called the Thyia,

s: Thyia is a festival (in honour of Dionysus)
q: their festival in his honour called the Thyia,

s: Thyia is celebrated at distance from Elis (about 8 stades)
q: a festival which they celebrate about 8 stades from the city.

s: Romans oppose Pyrrhus (in Italy)
q: for he knew that the Romans would not let him go scot-free

s: Antigonus fortifies the towns of the Macedonians
q: Antigonus having fortified the towns of the Macedonians pressed into the Peloponnese

s: Antigonus has troops defeated by Pyrrhus (including a Galatian contingent)
q: And having beaten Antigonus’ own troops, and the foreign contingent with him of the Galati

s: Epirus has ended glory of Epirus
q: Such was the end of the glory of Epirus.
